summary: Points out a security flaw in widely deployed resolvers: the way they add search suffixes to partial domain names can be exploited. The memo describes the flaw, a real case, and a fix.

eli5.summary: If you shorten an address and the post office guesses the rest, someone could trick it into guessing wrong. This memo shows the trick and how to stop it.

questions: dns resolver search list security problem
what is the dns search list vulnerability
why do resolvers limit search lists
what is a rooted domain name
subtitle: Resolver search lists could send a partial name to an unintended host outside the local administration.

tldr.problem: Resolvers based on BSD BIND tried partial names against a search list built from the searching host's own domain name, so a lookup could be intercepted by a domain outside local control.
tldr.mechanism: The memo says resolvers must honor the boundary between local and public administration, limiting search lists to the locally administered part of the name space and not shipping with implicit or explicit lists that go beyond it.
tldr.outcome: BIND 4.9.2 already narrows its implicit search list to the first and last candidate, and other search rules must be configured explicitly.

facts.label: Fixed in
facts.value: BIND 4.9.2 narrows the implicit search list

today: RFC 1535 is Informational and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It documents a flaw and a proposed correction, not a standard.

sections.title: How Partial Names Get Completed
sections.content:
Resolvers translate human-readable names into addresses. An absolute, rooted name ends in a dot; a non-rooted name does not. Many widely distributed resolvers based on BSD BIND resolve a partial name by walking a search list of domains and adding them to the name until a record is found. The memo notes this feature is disabled by default in the official BIND 4.9.2 release.

For example, a user on Machine.Tech.ACES.COM connecting to UnivHost.University.EDU would see these tried in order: UnivHost.University.EDU.Tech.ACES.COM., then UnivHost.University.EDU.ACES.COM., then UnivHost.University.EDU.COM., then UnivHost.University.EDU.
sections.eli5: If you leave off part of an address, the computer tries adding different endings until one works.

sections.title: The Security Flaw
sections.content:
After the EDU.COM domain was registered, it was found that one wildcard CNAME record would make all connections from any .COM site to any .EDU site end at one machine in the private edu.com subdomain. Specific names registered there could also be used to spoof a host, for example harvard.edu.com pointing at a target host that shows a Harvard.edu login banner.

The root cause is that resolvers do not distinguish the locally administered part of their own domain name from the publicly administered part, so the search can be intercepted while walking up the list. The memo calls this entirely unacceptable when it affects users outside the local administration.
sections.eli5: Someone can buy an ending that gets added to everyone's shortened addresses and send them to a fake place.

sections.title: The Proposed Correction
sections.content:
At a minimum, resolvers must honor the boundary between local and public administration by limiting search lists to the locally administered portion. Resolvers SHOULD NOT use implicit search lists other than the host's immediate parent domain, and those that still use them MUST limit their scope to locally administered subdomains. Resolvers SHOULD NOT come pre-configured with explicit search lists that perpetuate the problem.

If a name contains a dot it should be assumed to be a fully qualified name and SHOULD be tried as a rooted name first. BIND 4.9.2 tries only the first and last candidates from an implicit list, and extra search rules must be configured explicitly, which can break organizations that rely on multi-part partial names.
sections.eli5: Only add endings from your own street, never from the whole town, and try the full address first if it has dots.
